subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 17 periods = 680 minutes
Total: 17 periods · 11h 20min

periods.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students look at the pictures of animals, birds, insects, and plants and discuss which of these live in their homes (p. 73)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of myna, hibiscus, dragonfly, cat, snail, goat, grasshopper, and potted plants (p. 73)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 73 and study the illustration quietly. The teacher invites one or two children to name what they see before the discussion begins.

Whole-class discussion: which of these animals, birds, insects, and plants live in your home? Do your families take care of them? The teacher listens for both invited and uninvited guests that children mention and holds the contrast lightly without resolving it yet.

Children talk with a partner about an elder in their family — a grandparent, aunt, or neighbour — who kept a particular animal or plant when they were young. Each pair shares one story with the class, surfacing intergenerational knowledge about living with other creatures.

Children use Textbook p. 73 to begin the table: animals, birds, and insects they have spotted that are not in the picture. They write the name and where they saw it. Those who finish early add a second entry.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify living things they share their immediate environment with and describe how families care for them.
periods.section_context: Myna, hibiscus, dragonfly, cat, snail, goat, grasshopper, potted plants; invited versus uninvited living things in the home; elders' memories of animals and plants they kept.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did your dadi or nani or any older person at home ever tell you about an animal or plant they loved when they were young?' This opens intergenerational conversation naturally. Group children so that those from different household types (apartment, farm, village) sit near each other.

periods.activity_title: Uninvited Guests — Why Do They Come?
periods.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students discuss which uninvited animals, birds, and insects visit their home and why they think they come (p. 74)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens by asking the class to close their eyes and picture their kitchen, bedroom, or garden at home. What creatures visit without being invited? Children call out names as they open their eyes — the teacher lists these on the board.

Discussion guided by Textbook p. 74: Which uninvited animals, birds, and insects visit your home? Why do they come? Children reason aloud — food, warmth, shelter, water. The teacher encourages children to say what each creature might be looking for rather than labelling it a pest.

Discussion continues: How do you feel about these uninvited guests? Which ones do you like? What do you do when you do not like them? The teacher guides the group toward recognising that even discomfort does not mean the creature is harmful, building gentle empathy.

Children draw a quick two-column table in their notebooks: 'I like' and 'I do not like'. They fill in two or three uninvited creatures in each column and write one word next to each saying why. The teacher circulates and asks about their choices.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain why living things enter shared spaces and describe their own responses to those they welcome and those they do not.
periods.section_context: Uninvited animals, birds, and insects in the home; reasons creatures visit human spaces (food, warmth, shelter); children's feelings and responses toward uninvited living things.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When a child says they kill or shoo away an animal, ask gently: 'What do you think that creature was looking for?' — this nudges the group toward the creature's perspective without moralising. Seat children in mixed groups so rural and urban experiences appear in every cluster.

periods.activity_title: The Mango Tree Story — One Tree, Many Lives
periods.textbook_anchor: The Mango Tree — Students read the story of Shambhu and his father and discuss how we are dependent on plants and animals (p. 77)
periods.visual_aids: Radial diagram of uses of plants in the textbook (p. 77)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the story of Shambhu and his father aloud while children follow in Textbook p. 77. The teacher pauses after each creature appears — bird, squirrel, monkey — and asks children what that creature is doing in the tree.

Children examine the radial diagram of plant uses on Textbook p. 77. In pairs they identify which use matters most to their own family and share with the class. The discussion surfaces how plants are connected to medicine, food, clothing, and shelter in children's own homes.

Discussion: How are we dependent on plants and animals? How do plants help animals, and animals help plants? Children contribute examples from the story and from their own experience. The teacher draws a simple web on the board showing the connections as children name them.
Children write two sentences in their notebooks: one about how a plant helps an animal, and one about how an animal helps a plant, using examples from the story or from their own knowledge.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe relationships of mutual support between plants, animals, and humans using examples from their environment.
periods.section_context: Mango tree as shared habitat for birds, squirrels, monkeys; seed dispersal by monkeys; uses of plants — shade, wood, medicine, fibre, fruit, fresh air, shelter for animals; human dependence on plants and animals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do you know any plant that your family uses for medicine or for making something at home?' — this invites children to connect the radial diagram to their own household knowledge. Pause on the monkey-and-seed moment to let the ecological idea of unintentional seed dispersal land before moving on.

periods.activity_title: How Do We Look After Plants and Animals?
periods.textbook_anchor: The Mango Tree — Students discuss how they look after plants and animals in their surroundings and how animals and plants depend on us (p. 77)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a quiet moment: 'Think of one plant or animal near your home or school. What does it need from you?' Children sit with the thought for a short while before sharing.

Discussion from Textbook p. 77: How do you look after plants and animals in your surroundings? How do animals and plants depend on us? Children describe watering plants, feeding animals, keeping spaces clean, leaving water out in summer. The teacher affirms each as an act of care.

The teacher asks: 'What would happen to the animals or plants near your home if no one looked after them?' Children reason through consequences, connecting care to survival. The group builds a shared understanding that care is reciprocal.
Children write a short personal commitment in their notebooks: 'I will take care of ___ by ___.' The teacher circulates and asks each child to say their commitment aloud quietly to a neighbour.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe specific actions they take to support the needs of plants and animals in their immediate environment.
periods.section_context: Human care for plants and animals — watering, feeding, sheltering; dependence of animals and plants on human action; responsibility toward living things in one's surroundings.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone in your family ever told you about how people in your village or neighbourhood have always looked after a particular tree or animal?' — this invites community-level care practices to surface. Keep the mood reflective and unhurried; this unit is about disposition, not information.

periods.activity_title: What Animals Give Us and What We Give Them
periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students discuss how humans and animals depend on each other through care, food, shelter, and seed dispersal (p. 78)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of cow, buffalo, goat, and domesticated animals providing milk and companionship (p. 78)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 78 and examine the illustrations. The teacher asks: 'What do you see? What are the people doing with the animals? What are the animals doing?' Children describe the scene before any explanation.

Discussion: What do humans give animals — protection, food, shelter? What do animals give humans — milk, wool, companionship, help with soil? The teacher builds a two-sided list on the board as children contribute. The 'Do you know?' panel about squirrels burying and forgetting nuts is read aloud and discussed.

Children discuss how animals help plants — carrying seeds, making soil fertile through waste. The teacher uses simple questions: 'Where do seeds go when an animal eats a fruit and walks away?' The concept of unintentional service by animals is explored playfully.
Children draw a quick three-box diagram in their notebooks labelled 'Humans give animals', 'Animals give humans', 'Animals help plants', and write one example in each box using the discussion.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain the mutual benefits exchanged between humans, animals, and plants using everyday examples.
periods.section_context: Cows, buffaloes, goats providing milk; animals providing shelter material, clothing fibre, companionship; seed dispersal and soil fertility through animal waste; squirrels burying and forgetting nuts; mutual care and protection.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone at home keep a cow, goat, or bird? What does your family give it and what does it give your family?' — this grounds the mutual dependence concept in children's lived experience. The squirrel-and-nuts panel often delights Grade III children; let them laugh and then ask what this shows us.

periods.activity_title: Get to Know an Animal — Close Observation
periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students choose an animal they see often and observe it closely, noting its behaviour, movement, and sounds (p. 78)
materials: Bowl of water and grains (optional, if an animal is accessible)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the 'Get to Know an Animal' activity from Textbook p. 78 aloud. Children choose one animal or bird they see regularly — a crow, sparrow, goat, dog, cat, pigeon, or any other — and write its name in their notebook.

If an animal or bird is observable from the classroom or school campus, children observe it quietly for an extended period, noting movement, sound, eating behaviour, and social interactions. If no live animal is available, children close their eyes and recall a recent observation in as much detail as possible before writing.

Children write a structured description in their notebooks following the prompts from Textbook p. 78: name and appearance, when and where they first saw it, whether it was alone or with others, how it moved, what sounds it made, what it was doing, and anything that surprised or amused them.
Two or three children share their description aloud. The class listens and asks one question each. The teacher notes the variety of animals chosen on the board.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record structured observations of an animal's behaviour, movement, and sounds using their own experience as the data source.
periods.section_context: Observation of a chosen animal — goat, cow, dog, cat, crow, pigeon, sparrow, parrot, duck; animal movement, sounds, feeding behaviour, social interactions; keeping water and grains for an animal.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did anything the animal did surprise you or make you laugh? What do you think it was feeling at that moment?' — this lifts the observation beyond physical description into empathetic attention. Allow an unhurried writing phase; children who write slowly benefit from dictating to a partner.

periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students write a short description of the animal or bird they observed and share their story with classmates (p. 78)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 78 and re-read the writing prompts. The teacher explains that each child will prepare a short spoken story about their chosen animal — not just facts, but what they felt and noticed. A brief model is given orally by the teacher.

Children refine or complete their written description from their notebooks, ensuring they have addressed movement, sound, feeding, social behaviour, and one surprising moment. Those who finish early may add a small sketch of the animal at the top of their page.

Children share their stories in small groups of four, taking turns as speaker and listener. Each listener asks one question after the story. The teacher moves from group to group, listening for rich observations and encouraging quieter children.
The teacher invites one or two children to share a single surprising detail from their story with the whole class. The teacher closes by noting the variety of animals the class has observed together.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present observations of a living creature through written and oral description, including behaviour, movement, sound, and personal response.
periods.section_context: Written and oral descriptions of observed animals — goat, cow, dog, cat, crow, pigeon, sparrow, parrot, duck; movement, sounds, feeding, social behaviour, surprising or amusing moments; sharing stories with classmates.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups: 'What was the most surprising thing someone's animal did?' — this keeps listening active and purposeful. If a child has not had a chance to observe a live animal, their recalled memory or a family story counts fully.

periods.activity_title: Busy, Busy, Clever Ants — Making Predictions
periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students set up the Busy, Busy, Clever Ants experiment: three food types placed on the floor, with predictions made before observation (p. 79)
materials: Small amounts of sweet food (sugar or jaggery)
Small amounts of fried food (papad or murukku)
Small amounts of cooked food (bread, chapati, idli, rice, or ragi)
Sheets of paper or plates to place food on

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the 'Busy, Busy, Busy and Clever Ants!' activity from Textbook p. 79 aloud. Children help identify the three food types from the list and confirm they have brought or been given small quantities of each. The setup is explained clearly.

Children (in small groups or as a class, depending on space) set up three food samples on the floor in a straight line with equal gaps between them. Each group records the names of the three foods in their notebook.

Before any ants arrive, children answer each prediction question from Textbook p. 79 in their notebooks: Who will come? Which will be their favourite food? Will any ants come? Where will they come from? Will all ants look the same? Which food will they go to first? How many will come? What will they do with the food?

Children begin observing quietly, noting what actually happens. The teacher encourages them to whisper observations to a neighbour rather than calling out, maintaining a calm inquiry atmosphere. Observations are jotted briefly.

periods.implied_lo: Students can make explicit predictions about animal behaviour before an observation, framing each as a question to be tested.
periods.section_context: Ant experiment setup; three food types — sweet (sugar, jaggery), fried (papad, murukku), cooked (bread, chapati, idli, rice, ragi); eight prediction questions about ant behaviour, arrival, food preference, appearance, and quantity.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why did you predict that food? What do you know about ants that made you think that?' — this surfaces prior knowledge and makes the prediction a reasoned one, not a guess. Ensure each group records predictions before the ants arrive so comparison is possible.

periods.activity_title: Busy, Busy, Clever Ants — Observing and Comparing
periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students observe ant behaviour and compare what they see with their earlier predictions (p. 79)
materials: Food samples from the experiment (or fresh samples if set up anew)

time_bands.activity: Children set up the three food types again (or return to the previous setup if ants are still active). They open their notebooks to their prediction page. The teacher reminds them that the task now is to observe carefully and record what they actually see — not what they expected.

An extended, unhurried observation period: children watch the food samples and record observations against each prediction question. They note which food attracted ants, whether ants look the same, what the ants do with the food, and where they seem to come from. The teacher moves quietly, prompting with: 'Look carefully — what exactly are the ants doing with that piece of food?'

Children compare their written predictions with their observations, putting a tick next to predictions that matched and a cross next to those that did not. They write one sentence: 'I was surprised that ___.' The teacher collects a range of these surprises on the board.

Brief whole-class discussion: What did the ants teach us about how animals make choices? The teacher connects ant food preference to the chapter's broader idea of animals having their own needs and behaviours.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare predictions about animal behaviour with observed outcomes and identify what was unexpected.
periods.section_context: Ant observation — which food attracted ants, ant appearance, ant behaviour with food, origin of ant trail, quantity of ants; comparing predictions to actual observations; surprise findings from the experiment.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did all ants in your group look exactly the same? Did any carry food alone or together?' — this draws attention to detail and social behaviour in ants. If ants did not arrive, ask children to reason about why they might not have and what they could change next time — this keeps the inquiry spirit alive.

periods.activity_title: Visiting Your Plant Friend — Empathy Through Care
periods.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students explore the practice of visiting a plant when feeling sad, angry, or happy, and understand that plants also need care and support (p. 80)
materials: A potted plant or access to a school garden (if available)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration from p. 80 showing a child with a plant

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the 'Visiting your Plant Friend' section from Textbook p. 80 aloud slowly. Children listen with their eyes closed. Afterward, the teacher asks: 'Have you ever sat near a plant or tree when you were feeling something strongly?'

Discussion: Why might someone visit a plant when they are sad, angry, or happy? What does it feel like to sit near a tree or a plant you know well? Children share personal experiences freely. The teacher holds the space without rushing to a lesson — the feeling itself is the content.

Children go quietly to a plant in the classroom or school garden (or recall their favourite plant if going outside is not possible). They spend an unhurried time with the plant — looking at it closely, touching a leaf gently, or simply sitting near it. They return and write two or three sentences: 'My plant friend is ___ and it makes me feel ___ because ___.'

Children share their sentences in a circle, one by one. The teacher closes by reading the chapter's statement aloud: 'Plants also need our care and support. So do animals. We can all help each other.' The group sits with this quietly for a moment.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express the emotional and reciprocal dimension of caring for a plant, describing what a plant needs and what it gives in return.
periods.section_context: Visiting a plant when feeling sad, upset, angry, or happy; plant as friend needing care and support; emotional reciprocity between humans and plants; school or home plants.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone know of a family or community tradition where a particular plant or tree is treated with special respect or care?' — this opens space for local cultural practices around sacred trees, medicinal plants, or festival plants without directing the answer. Keep the atmosphere calm and unhurried throughout.

periods.activity_title: Guess Who I Am? — Moving Like Living Things
periods.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students play 'Guess Who I Am?' in pairs, miming the movement of an animal, bird, insect, or tree for the class to guess (p. 80)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the 'Guess Who I Am?' activity from Textbook p. 80 aloud and demonstrates one mime herself — perhaps a crow hopping and cawing — without saying what she is. Children guess. The rules are clarified: whisper, mime, guess, switch.

Children sit in pairs. One whispers a living thing (animal, bird, insect, or tree) to their partner. The partner mimes the movement, and the class guesses. Pairs take several rounds, switching roles each time. The teacher facilitates turns so all pairs get a chance and gently steers children toward a wide variety of living things — not just popular animals.

Brief discussion: What was the hardest living thing to mime? What made it hard? How did your body know how to move like that creature? The teacher connects bodily knowledge to observation — we can only mime what we have truly watched.
Children write the name of the living thing they found hardest to mime in their notebooks and one sentence about what they would need to observe to mime it better.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express their knowledge of a living thing's distinctive movement and behaviour through bodily mime.
periods.section_context: Mime game — animals, birds, insects, trees; bodily expression of movement and behaviour of living things; pair activity with class guessing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'How did you know how to move like that? Have you watched this creature closely?' — this links expressive play back to observation as a foundation. Encourage children to mime less common creatures — a snail, a dragonfly, a banyan tree in wind — not only crowd-pleasers like dogs and cats.

periods.activity_title: The Valparai Welcome — A Community's Harmony with Nature
periods.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students discuss the 'Do you know?' panel about school children and teachers in Valparai welcoming migratory Grey Wagtails each winter (p. 80)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook 'Do you know?' panel featuring the Grey Wagtail tradition in Valparai (p. 80)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the 'Do you know?' panel from Textbook p. 80 aloud — the story of children and teachers in Valparai, Tamil Nadu, who track the Grey Wagtail's arrival every winter and celebrate with welcome posters and sweets. The teacher pauses and asks: 'What do you think — why did these children decide to welcome a bird?'

Discussion: What does this tradition tell us about how humans can celebrate their relationship with nature? Does your family or community have any tradition or practice around welcoming a season, a bird, a flower, or a tree? Children share local examples freely — harvest festivals, sacred trees, seasonal fruits.

Children design a simple welcome poster in their notebooks for a bird, insect, animal, or plant that arrives in their area in a particular season or that they particularly love. They write the creature's name, draw it, and write one welcoming sentence underneath.
Children share their posters in small groups. The teacher asks: 'If your school decided to welcome this creature every year, what would you do?' Groups share one idea each with the class.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how a community practice expresses care for and connection with a living creature, and connect it to practices in their own environment.
periods.section_context: Valparai, Tamil Nadu; Grey Wagtail (Vaalatti kuruvi); winter arrival of migratory birds; school children and teachers making welcome posters and distributing sweets; community celebration of human-nature harmony.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do you know a bird, animal, or plant that comes to your area only at a certain time of year? Does your family do anything special when it arrives?' — this draws out local seasonal knowledge and cultural practices. Avoid positioning the Valparai tradition as the only or best example; it is an opening, not a model to copy.

periods.activity_title: How Are We Dependent on Plants and Animals? — Reflection Discussion
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss how we are dependent on plants and animals and how they depend on us (p. 81)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 81. The teacher reads the three 'Let us reflect' discussion questions aloud: How are we dependent on plants and animals? How should we care for them? How do plants and animals depend on us? Children read them again silently and mark the one they feel most strongly about.

Small-group discussion (groups of three): each group takes one question and prepares a brief response to share. The teacher circulates, listening for examples that are concrete and local — a particular plant, a familiar animal, a real caregiving action.

Whole-class sharing: each group presents their discussion. The teacher holds the three questions on the board and builds a shared web of dependencies — humans need plants and animals; plants and animals need humans; all are bound together. Children add to the web as ideas arise.
Children write one sentence in their notebooks completing the idea: 'We depend on ___ and in return we must ___.' The teacher reads a few aloud to close.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate specific ways humans depend on plants and animals and specific ways those living things depend on human care.
periods.section_context: Human dependence on plants and animals; care for plants and animals in the environment; dependence of plants and animals on humans; reflection on mutual responsibility.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you think of a plant or animal near your home that would suffer if people stopped caring for it? What would change?' — this makes the abstract idea of dependence concrete and personal. Allow each group to use a different example so the class web is genuinely varied.

periods.activity_title: Living Beings I Love — Sentence Completion and Favourites
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students complete sentence frames expressing personal connection to living beings they love and write about their favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant (p. 81)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 81 and read the four sentence frames silently: 'I like looking at ___ because ___', '___ make me laugh because ___', 'My friend ___ likes ___ because ___', 'I would like to take care of ___ because ___'. The teacher reads them aloud slowly, leaving space for children to think.

Children complete all four sentence frames in their notebooks, choosing their own living beings. The teacher encourages children to choose different living things for each sentence — not the same animal four times. Those who finish quickly add a small sketch.

Children answer the favourite-animal questions from Textbook p. 81: Which is your favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant from those you have named? Why do you like it? They write two to three sentences giving a genuine reason, not just 'it is beautiful'.

Children share their sentence completions in pairs, then one or two volunteers share with the class. The teacher notes the variety of living beings chosen across the class — celebrating the breadth of connections the group has with the natural world.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express personal emotional connections to living beings through structured written sentences, giving reasons for their feelings.
periods.section_context: Sentence frames about living beings — 'I like looking at', 'make me laugh', 'my friend likes', 'I would like to take care of'; favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant and reasons for liking it.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you write about a living being that not many people in the class might choose? Something small or ordinary that you find interesting?' — this broadens the range of creatures children value. Avoid correcting grammar in these expressive sentences during the sharing phase; the connection matters more.

periods.activity_title: Smallest to Largest — Ranking Living Things
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students write the names of all the animals, birds, and insects they have seen or learned about from smallest to largest (p. 81)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens by asking: 'If we lined up all the animals, birds, and insects in this room — all the ones we have talked about, drawn, mimed, and observed — from smallest to largest, where would you start? Where would you end?' Children suggest extreme cases (ant, elephant) to anchor the scale.

Children individually write a ranked list in their notebooks from Textbook p. 81: all the animals, birds, and insects they have seen or learned about, from smallest to largest. They use their own observations and memory. The teacher encourages them to include the tiny — ants, snails, dragonflies — not only large familiar animals.

Children compare their lists with a partner: where do their lists differ? Did one person rank a sparrow smaller than a cat? Did they agree on where a goat sits? The discussion surfaces the challenge of size comparison across types of creatures.

The teacher asks two or three children to share the creature they found hardest to place in order and why. The class discusses briefly, recognising that ranking living things requires careful observation — not just names.

periods.implied_lo: Students can order a set of living things by size, drawing on direct observation and prior knowledge to justify their ranking.
periods.section_context: Ranking animals, birds, and insects from smallest to largest; creatures encountered or studied — ant, snail, dragonfly, sparrow, cat, goat, crow, cow; size comparison across creature types.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'How do you know this creature is bigger than that one? Have you seen them side by side?' — this pushes children to distinguish between remembered size and assumed size. Accept varied rankings as long as children can give a reason; there is no single correct order for middle-sized creatures.

periods.activity_title: How Many Legs? — Drawing and Classifying Living Things
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students name and draw animals, birds, and insects that have two, four, six, and eight legs (p. 82)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 82 and read the draw task: name and draw animals, birds, and insects with two legs, four legs, six legs, and eight legs. The teacher asks: 'Before you draw, think — do you actually know how many legs an ant has? A spider? A bee?' Children make quick mental checks.

Children create a four-section page in their notebooks — one section per leg count — and draw and name at least one creature in each section. The teacher encourages them to recall every creature from the chapter and from their own experience. Those who draw quickly are invited to add more creatures to each section.

Children walk around the room in a gallery format, looking at two or three classmates' drawings and checking: 'Did they put the right creatures in the right sections?' They whisper any disagreements to the artist who can check and correct. The teacher facilitates: 'Did anyone put something unexpected in the six-legs section?'
The teacher closes by asking: 'Why does it help to sort living things by how many legs they have? What does it tell us about them?' A brief exchange grounds the classification act in a purpose.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify living things by number of legs and represent that classification through named drawings.
periods.section_context: Two-legged creatures — birds (crow, sparrow, pigeon, parrot, duck, myna); four-legged — cat, dog, goat, cow, squirrel; six-legged — ants, grasshoppers, dragonflies; eight-legged — spiders; drawing and naming examples in each category.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Are you sure about that one? How could you check?' — this keeps classification as an inquiry, not a memory exercise. Watch for the common confusion between insects (six legs) and spiders (eight legs); let children discover and discuss it rather than correcting it directly.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students complete sentence frames expressing personal connection to living beings and their care, drawing together the chapter's ideas (p. 81)
materials: Large sheets of paper or notebook pages

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a broad question: 'If you had to explain to a younger child what "Living in Harmony" means, what would you say? What living things are part of it? What do humans do? What do animals and plants do?' Children think quietly and then share brief ideas. The teacher notes key phrases on the board: care, dependence, seed dispersal, soil, welcome, observe, classify.

Children create a personal 'Harmony Map' on a large sheet of paper or a full notebook page. At the centre they write or draw themselves. Around them they place: living things they share their home with, living things in their surroundings, plants they have a relationship with, and animals they have observed. They draw arrows showing what each gives and receives — food, shelter, care, seeds, soil, companionship — using words and drawings together. The map may draw on any of the chapter's concepts: mutual dependence between humans and animals, seed dispersal, the mango tree's services, the ant experiment's lesson about animal preferences, the migratory bird welcome tradition, or classification by legs.

Children write three sentences below their map: one about something a plant gives that humans depend on, one about something an animal does that helps the natural world, and one about one action they personally take — or would like to take — to care for a living being. The teacher moves through the room, asking each child to read one sentence aloud quietly.

A closing circle: each child says one word that describes what 'living in harmony' means to them. The teacher records the words on the board. The lesson closes with the board full of the class's own language about the chapter's central idea.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent the web of mutual dependence between humans, animals, and plants through a visual map and articulate personal responsibility within that web.
periods.section_context: Whole-chapter synthesis: living things sharing human spaces; invited and uninvited animals; mango tree as shared habitat; uses of plants; mutual care and dependence; seed dispersal and soil fertility; ant food preferences; visiting a plant friend; Valparai Grey Wagtail welcome tradition; sentence frames about living beings; ranking by size; classification by leg count.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Look at your map — is there any living thing on it that depends on you? What would change for that creature if you were not there?' — this makes personal responsibility visible and concrete. Accept all forms of the Harmony Map: those with many arrows and those with few, those heavily illustrated and those mostly written.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify living things they share their immediate environment with and describe how families care for them.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Myna, hibiscus, dragonfly, cat, snail, goat, grasshopper, potted plants; invited versus uninvited living things in the home; elders' memories of animals and plants they kept.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students look at the pictures of animals, birds, insects, and plants and discuss which of these live in their homes (p. 73)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students examine the textbook illustration and discuss which living things share their home, then record animals they have spotted that are not in the picture.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why living things enter shared spaces and describe their own responses to those they welcome and those they do not.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Uninvited animals, birds, and insects in the home; reasons creatures visit human spaces (food, warmth, shelter); children's feelings and responses toward uninvited living things.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students discuss which uninvited animals, birds, and insects visit their home and why they think they come (p. 74)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss uninvited creatures in their home, explore why they come, and record feelings toward them in a two-column notebook table.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe relationships of mutual support between plants, animals, and humans using examples from their environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Mango tree as shared habitat for birds, squirrels, monkeys; seed dispersal by monkeys; uses of plants — shade, wood, medicine, fibre, fruit, fresh air, shelter for animals; human dependence on plants and animals.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: The Mango Tree — Students read the story of Shambhu and his father and discuss how we are dependent on plants and animals (p. 77)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students follow the Shambhu story, examine the radial diagram of plant uses, and discuss mutual dependence between plants, animals, and humans.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe specific actions they take to support the needs of plants and animals in their immediate environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Human care for plants and animals — watering, feeding, sheltering; dependence of animals and plants on human action; responsibility toward living things in one's surroundings.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: The Mango Tree — Students discuss how they look after plants and animals in their surroundings and how animals and plants depend on us (p. 77)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students reflect on how they care for plants and animals in their surroundings and write a personal commitment to one act of care.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain the mutual benefits exchanged between humans, animals, and plants using everyday examples.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Cows, buffaloes, goats providing milk; animals providing shelter material, clothing fibre, companionship; seed dispersal and soil fertility through animal waste; squirrels burying and forgetting nuts; mutual care and protection.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students discuss how humans and animals depend on each other through care, food, shelter, and seed dispersal (p. 78)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students examine illustrations of domestic animals, discuss what humans and animals give each other, and explore how animals help plants spread and grow.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can record structured observations of an animal's behaviour, movement, and sounds using their own experience as the data source.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Observation of a chosen animal — goat, cow, dog, cat, crow, pigeon, sparrow, parrot, duck; animal movement, sounds, feeding behaviour, social interactions; keeping water and grains for an animal.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students choose an animal they see often and observe it closely, noting its behaviour, movement, and sounds (p. 78)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students choose one familiar animal, observe or recall it closely, and write a structured description covering appearance, movement, sounds, feeding, and a surprising moment.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can present observations of a living creature through written and oral description, including behaviour, movement, sound, and personal response.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Written and oral descriptions of observed animals — goat, cow, dog, cat, crow, pigeon, sparrow, parrot, duck; movement, sounds, feeding, social behaviour, surprising or amusing moments; sharing stories with classmates.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students write a short description of the animal or bird they observed and share their story with classmates (p. 78)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students refine their written animal description and share it orally in small groups, listening and asking questions in response to each other's stories.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can make explicit predictions about animal behaviour before an observation, framing each as a question to be tested.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Ant experiment setup; three food types — sweet (sugar, jaggery), fried (papad, murukku), cooked (bread, chapati, idli, rice, ragi); eight prediction questions about ant behaviour, arrival, food preference, appearance, and quantity.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students set up the Busy, Busy, Clever Ants experiment: three food types placed on the floor, with predictions made before observation (p. 79)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students set up three food samples, record predictions for all eight inquiry questions about ant behaviour, and begin initial observations.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can compare predictions about animal behaviour with observed outcomes and identify what was unexpected.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Ant observation — which food attracted ants, ant appearance, ant behaviour with food, origin of ant trail, quantity of ants; comparing predictions to actual observations; surprise findings from the experiment.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students observe ant behaviour and compare what they see with their earlier predictions (p. 79)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe ant behaviour at the three food samples, compare each observation with their written prediction, and identify one thing that surprised them.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can express the emotional and reciprocal dimension of caring for a plant, describing what a plant needs and what it gives in return.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Visiting a plant when feeling sad, upset, angry, or happy; plant as friend needing care and support; emotional reciprocity between humans and plants; school or home plants.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students explore the practice of visiting a plant when feeling sad, angry, or happy, and understand that plants also need care and support (p. 80)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students read and discuss the 'Visiting your Plant Friend' section, spend quiet time with a plant, and write sentences about what their plant friend means to them.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can express their knowledge of a living thing's distinctive movement and behaviour through bodily mime.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Mime game — animals, birds, insects, trees; bodily expression of movement and behaviour of living things; pair activity with class guessing.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students play 'Guess Who I Am?' in pairs, miming the movement of an animal, bird, insect, or tree for the class to guess (p. 80)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students play 'Guess Who I Am?' in pairs, miming living things for the class to identify, then reflect on what close observation enables bodily expression.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe how a community practice expresses care for and connection with a living creature, and connect it to practices in their own environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Valparai, Tamil Nadu; Grey Wagtail (Vaalatti kuruvi); winter arrival of migratory birds; school children and teachers making welcome posters and distributing sweets; community celebration of human-nature harmony.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students discuss the 'Do you know?' panel about school children and teachers in Valparai welcoming migratory Grey Wagtails each winter (p. 80)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students read the Valparai Grey Wagtail story, discuss community traditions of welcoming nature, and design a simple welcome poster for a creature in their own environment.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can articulate specific ways humans depend on plants and animals and specific ways those living things depend on human care.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Human dependence on plants and animals; care for plants and animals in the environment; dependence of plants and animals on humans; reflection on mutual responsibility.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss how we are dependent on plants and animals and how they depend on us (p. 81)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss the three 'Let us reflect' questions in small groups, build a shared web of dependencies on the board, and write a sentence about reciprocal responsibility.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can express personal emotional connections to living beings through structured written sentences, giving reasons for their feelings.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Sentence frames about living beings — 'I like looking at', 'make me laugh', 'my friend likes', 'I would like to take care of'; favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant and reasons for liking it.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students complete sentence frames expressing personal connection to living beings they love and write about their favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant (p. 81)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students complete four sentence frames about living beings they love and write a short paragraph about their favourite creature with genuine reasons.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can order a set of living things by size, drawing on direct observation and prior knowledge to justify their ranking.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Ranking animals, birds, and insects from smallest to largest; creatures encountered or studied — ant, snail, dragonfly, sparrow, cat, goat, crow, cow; size comparison across creature types.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students write the names of all the animals, birds, and insects they have seen or learned about from smallest to largest (p. 81)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students independently rank all living things they have encountered from smallest to largest, compare rankings with a partner, and discuss points of disagreement.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify living things by number of legs and represent that classification through named drawings.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Two-legged creatures — birds (crow, sparrow, pigeon, parrot, duck, myna); four-legged — cat, dog, goat, cow, squirrel; six-legged — ants, grasshoppers, dragonflies; eight-legged — spiders; drawing and naming examples in each category.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students name and draw animals, birds, and insects that have two, four, six, and eight legs (p. 82)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students create a four-section drawing page classifying creatures by leg count, walk the room in a gallery format to check each other's classifications, and discuss why classification is useful.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can represent the web of mutual dependence between humans, animals, and plants through a visual map and articulate personal responsibility within that web.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Whole-chapter synthesis: living things sharing human spaces; invited and uninvited animals; mango tree as shared habitat; uses of plants; mutual care and dependence; seed dispersal and soil fertility; ant food preferences; visiting a plant friend; Valparai Grey Wagtail welcome tradition; sentence frames about living beings; ranking by size; classification by leg count.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students complete sentence frames expressing personal connection to living beings and their care, drawing together the chapter's ideas (p. 81)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students create a personal Harmony Map placing themselves at the centre of a web of living things, draw arrows of mutual giving and receiving, and write three synthesis sentences about dependence, animal service to nature, and personal care responsibility.

assessment_items.question_text: A family keeps a pot of hibiscus near their front door and allows a cat to sleep on their balcony. Which word best describes the hibiscus and the cat?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The distinction between invited and uninvited living things is the section's opening conceptual anchor.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify living things they share their immediate environment with and describe how families care for them.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has reversed the chapter's invited/uninvited distinction, applying 'uninvited' to animals the family has deliberately brought in — indicating the opening concept was not fully grasped.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is using a general category ('wild') that does not match the chapter's framing, suggesting they are drawing on prior knowledge rather than the section's specific language.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is associating animals sharing human space with harm — a reaction the chapter explicitly challenges — indicating the section's empathetic reframing has not registered.

assessment_items.question_text: Meena finds a lizard behind her kitchen shelf. She does not like it. According to what you have read and discussed, why is the lizard most likely there?

options.label: A
options.text: It came to harm Meena's family.

options.label: B
options.text: It is looking for food, warmth, or shelter.

options.label: C
options.text: It wants to live in the fridge.

options.label: D
options.text: It was invited by Meena's mother.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The section establishes that uninvited creatures come to human spaces because those spaces offer food, warmth, or shelter — not because they are harmful.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why living things enter shared spaces and describe their own responses to those they welcome and those they do not.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student holds onto the idea that uninvited animals are dangerous, which is the attitude the section directly challenges — indicating the empathy-building discussion did not shift their thinking.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused the invited/uninvited distinction, applying 'invited' where the section specifically frames the lizard as uninvited — suggesting the categories were not clearly understood.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has produced an implausible response, indicating either disengagement with the question or an inability to apply the section's reasoning about creature needs.

assessment_items.question_text: Shambhu and his father sat under a mango tree and watched many animals using it. Name two animals from the story and describe what each one was doing in the tree.
expected_elements: Names at least two animals from the story — bird, squirrel, or monkey.
Describes what each named animal was doing — for example, a bird nesting, a squirrel jumping between branches, a monkey eating a mango.
At least one description reflects the ecological role described in the section, such as the monkey eating a mango and throwing the seed.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for two animals with accurate, section-grounded descriptions of their activity. Award partial credit if two animals are named but descriptions are vague or absent. The monkey-and-seed detail is the section's key ecological insight — credit its inclusion.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe relationships of mutual support between plants, animals, and humans using examples from their environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

expected_elements: Names at least two animals from the story — bird, squirrel, or monkey.
Describes what each named animal was doing — for example, a bird nesting, a squirrel jumping between branches, a monkey eating a mango.
At least one description reflects the ecological role described in the section, such as the monkey eating a mango and throwing the seed.

assessment_items.task: Think of one plant or animal near your home or school. Draw it in the centre of your page. Around it, draw or write two things it needs from you and two things it gives you in return. Then write one sentence saying what you will do to take care of it.
assessment_items.scaffold: Centre drawing: [the plant or animal] | Around it: 'It needs from me: 1.___ 2.___' | 'It gives me: 1.___ 2.___' | My sentence: 'I will take care of ___ by ___.'
format_of_output: A central drawing of the chosen plant or animal
Two labelled needs of the creature from the student
Two labelled things the creature gives the student
One written sentence of personal commitment to care
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any plant or animal the child has genuine connection to. Regional variation is expected and appropriate — a coconut palm, a neem tree, a buffalo, a house sparrow are all equally valid. Credit the reasoning in the needs and gifts, not the choice of creature.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe specific actions they take to support the needs of plants and animals in their immediate environment.

competency.competency_text: Identifies needs of plants, birds, and animals, and how they can be supported (water, soil, food, care)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can identify what a specific living thing needs from humans and what it provides in return, and translate that understanding into a concrete personal commitment to care.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that the student has completed both the 'needs' and 'gives' sections — not just one direction of the relationship. The written sentence should name a specific action, not a vague intention.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: needs and gifts are specific and grounded (e.g. 'It needs water every day' / 'It gives me shade'), commitment is concrete (e.g. 'I will water it every morning'). Weak: needs and gifts are generic ('care', 'love'), commitment is absent or vague.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find drawing difficult may write all four items as words. Children who cannot think of a plant or animal at home may use one from their school campus or from the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Visual map with written labels and one sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The visual map mirrors the chapter's radial diagram of plant uses and makes the relationship between the student and the living thing concrete and visible.

assessment_items.question_text: Cows and goats give humans milk. What do humans give cows and goats in return? Give two examples.
expected_elements: Names at least one of: food, shelter, protection, water, care.
Names a second example distinct from the first.
The response reflects the chapter's framing of mutual dependence, not just listing random human actions.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for two distinct, section-grounded examples of what humans provide to domestic animals. Any combination of food, shelter, water, protection, and care is acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain the mutual benefits exchanged between humans, animals, and plants using everyday examples.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Names at least one of: food, shelter, protection, water, care.
Names a second example distinct from the first.
The response reflects the chapter's framing of mutual dependence, not just listing random human actions.

assessment_items.question_text: Aman watched a crow sitting on a wall near his school every afternoon. He noticed it tilted its head when a bell rang. What kind of activity was Aman doing?

options.label: A
options.text: He was carefully observing the crow's behaviour.

options.label: B
options.text: He was drawing the crow from a photograph.

options.label: D
options.text: He was scaring the crow away.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The unit's central skill is structured observation of an animal's behaviour in its own environment.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record structured observations of an animal's behaviour, movement, and sounds using their own experience as the data source.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses the act of providing care (feeding) with the act of attending to and recording what an animal does — suggesting the concept of observation as a distinct activity was not grasped.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student associates close attention to an animal with an attempt to remove it, which may reflect a default response to animals in shared spaces that the chapter's care activities were intended to shift.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student equates observation with copying an existing image rather than attending to a live creature, indicating a misunderstanding of direct observation as a primary source of data.

assessment_items.task: Write a short description of one animal or bird you have seen. Include: what it looks like, how it moves, what sounds it makes, and one thing it did that surprised or amused you. Then read your description to a partner.
assessment_items.scaffold: Name of animal or bird: ___ | What it looks like: ___ | How it moves: ___ | Sounds it makes: ___ | Something that surprised or amused me: ___ | (Read aloud to a partner when finished.)
format_of_output: Written description addressing all four prompt fields
One oral reading to a partner
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any animal or bird the student has genuinely observed. Regional variation is expected — a bulbul, a buffalo, a house sparrow, a crow, a lizard are all equally valid. Credit specificity and personal observation; deduct nothing for spelling. The oral component is observable when the teacher circulates.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present observations of a living creature through written and oral description, including behaviour, movement, sound, and personal response.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can transform a personal observation of a living creature into a structured written and oral description covering appearance, movement, sound, and a memorable moment.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Look for responses that go beyond naming the animal — movement, sound, and the surprise moment are the expressive core. A description that only names and describes size has not engaged with the observation prompts.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific details drawn from real observation (e.g. 'the sparrow hopped sideways before flying'), a distinct surprise moment, confident oral sharing. Weak: generic attributes ('it is small and brown'), no movement or sound description, no surprise moment.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who have not directly observed an animal recently may recall a vivid memory or use an animal from the chapter. Students who struggle with writing may dictate their description to the teacher or a peer.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Written description builds the structured observation skill; the oral reading mirrors the sharing-with-classmates requirement of the textbook task and develops spoken communication.

assessment_items.question_text: Before doing the ant experiment, Priya wrote: 'I think the ants will go to the sweet food first because ants like sugar.' What is this called?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The distinction between prediction (before) and observation (during) is the inquiry skill this unit centres on.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can make explicit predictions about animal behaviour before an observation, framing each as a question to be tested.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student conflates prediction with observation, not yet distinguishing the 'before' thinking from the 'during' watching — a core inquiry-process distinction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student conflates prediction with result, suggesting they see inquiry as linear reporting rather than a process where prediction precedes and is tested by observation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has associated scientific activity with drawing rather than with thinking/reasoning, suggesting the prediction-making step was not identified as a distinct cognitive act.

assessment_items.question_text: Ravi did the ant experiment. He predicted that ants would go to the sweet food first. He observed that the ants went to the cooked food first and ignored the sweet food. Write two things Ravi could write about what he found.
expected_elements: States what Ravi predicted — ants would go to the sweet food first.
States what Ravi observed — ants went to the cooked food first.
Identifies that the prediction and observation did not match, or names this as a surprise finding.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit when both the prediction and the observation are stated and their mismatch is noted. Award partial credit when only one of the two is addressed clearly.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare predictions about animal behaviour with observed outcomes and identify what was unexpected.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: States what Ravi predicted — ants would go to the sweet food first.
States what Ravi observed — ants went to the cooked food first.
Identifies that the prediction and observation did not match, or names this as a surprise finding.

assessment_items.task: Think of a plant you like — one near your home, school, or that you have visited. Write three sentences: one about what the plant needs from you or from nature, one about what it gives you or gives animals around it, and one about how you feel when you are near it.
assessment_items.scaffold: My plant: ___ | It needs: ___ | It gives: ___ | When I am near it, I feel: ___
format_of_output: Three written sentences — one for needs, one for giving, one for feeling
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any plant the student has genuine experience of. Regional variation is fully expected — a banana tree, a tulsi plant, a peepal, a mango tree, a vegetable in a kitchen garden are all valid. Credit the emotional sentence; it is the section's central contribution.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express the emotional and reciprocal dimension of caring for a plant, describing what a plant needs and what it gives in return.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can move beyond factual knowledge of plant needs to articulate the emotional and reciprocal quality of a human-plant relationship.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three sentences should be distinct — needs, giving, and feeling. A strong response will not repeat the same content across all three. The feeling sentence is the most telling indicator of this unit's learning.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: needs sentence is specific (e.g. 'it needs water and sunlight'), giving sentence includes something for animals as well as humans, feeling sentence is personal and specific (e.g. 'I feel calm'). Weak: all three sentences are factual with no emotional content, or only the needs sentence is completed.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who have never visited a plant knowingly may draw on the chapter's plant-friend concept and describe a tree they pass regularly. Children who struggle to write may dictate to the teacher.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The three-sentence structure mirrors the section's core message — care, reciprocity, and emotional connection — and keeps the task accessible for Grade III writers.

assessment_items.task: Choose one living thing — an animal, a bird, an insect, or a tree. Mime how it moves. Your teacher will watch as you perform your mime.
assessment_items.scaffold: Living thing I am miming: ___ (whispered to the teacher before performing). Perform the mime for the class.
format_of_output: A live bodily mime performance of the chosen living thing's movement
assessment_items.annotation: This is a performance task. The teacher observes the mime as it is performed. There is no written output to collect. Encourage children to choose creatures other than the most common ones (dog, cat) — credit the range and the specificity of the mime.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express their knowledge of a living thing's distinctive movement and behaviour through bodily mime.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate observation-based knowledge of a living thing into expressive bodily movement, demonstrating that they know how that creature moves and behaves.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The teacher notes the living thing the student whispers before performing and checks whether the mime communicates that creature's distinctive features — not a generic 'animal walk'.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: the mime captures a specific feature of the creature (a dragonfly's hovering, a snail's slowness, a crow's hopping and head-tilting), classmates can guess the creature. Weak: the mime is generic and could represent any animal, or the student declines to perform.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who are shy about performing alone may mime in a pair. Children with physical limitations may perform the mime seated, using arms and head rather than full body movement.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Bodily mime is the activity's own expressive mode — it cannot be replaced by writing without losing the unit's observational-kinesthetic link.
OPEN_TASK.observation_rubric: Watch for: (1) Does the mime show a movement pattern specific to the named creature, not a generic animal? (2) Can the teacher or class recognise the creature from the movement? (3) Does the student sustain the mime for a complete performance, not just a brief gesture?

assessment_items.question_text: In Valparai, Tamil Nadu, school children and teachers welcome the Grey Wagtail every winter. Describe one thing they do to welcome the bird and explain why you think they do it.
expected_elements: Names at least one welcoming action — making welcome posters or distributing sweets.
Gives a reason for the tradition — for example, they love the bird's arrival, they want to celebrate their relationship with nature, or they want the bird to feel welcomed.
The reason is grounded in the idea of human care for or connection with a living creature, not a factual error.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit when one welcoming action is correctly named and the reason given reflects care for or connection with the bird. Accept any reasonable interpretation of why the community does this — celebration of nature, love for the bird, community tradition.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how a community practice expresses care for and connection with a living creature, and connect it to practices in their own environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

expected_elements: Names at least one welcoming action — making welcome posters or distributing sweets.
Gives a reason for the tradition — for example, they love the bird's arrival, they want to celebrate their relationship with nature, or they want the bird to feel welcomed.
The reason is grounded in the idea of human care for or connection with a living creature, not a factual error.

assessment_items.question_text: Imagine your school has decided that every student must help take care of one plant and one animal near the school. What would you do for each, and why is it important?
look_for: Describes at least one specific care action for a plant (watering, removing dead leaves, ensuring sunlight).
Describes at least one specific care action for an animal (providing water, food, shelter, not disturbing it).
Gives a reason why this care matters — connected to the idea of mutual dependence or the living thing's need.
The response reflects the chapter's understanding that plants and animals depend on humans and that care is a responsibility, not just a kindness.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an extended reasoning item. Award full credit when both plant and animal care are addressed with specific actions and a reason grounded in mutual dependence. Award partial credit when only one living thing is addressed or when reasons are absent. Accept any regional plant or animal — the specific species does not matter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate specific ways humans depend on plants and animals and specific ways those living things depend on human care.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: Describes at least one specific care action for a plant (watering, removing dead leaves, ensuring sunlight).
Describes at least one specific care action for an animal (providing water, food, shelter, not disturbing it).
Gives a reason why this care matters — connected to the idea of mutual dependence or the living thing's need.
The response reflects the chapter's understanding that plants and animals depend on humans and that care is a responsibility, not just a kindness.

assessment_items.task:
Complete these two sentences with the names of real plants, animals, birds, or insects that you know. Write a reason for each one.
(a) I like looking at ___ because ___.
(b) I would like to take care of ___ because ___.
assessment_items.scaffold: (a) I like looking at ________ because ________. | (b) I would like to take care of ________ because ________.
format_of_output: Two completed sentence frames, each with a named living thing and a reason
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any living thing the student names — regional variety is expected and appropriate. A tulsi plant, a buffalo, a squirrel, a dragonfly are all valid. Credit the reason as the primary evidence of learning; 'because it is beautiful' is a weak reason — look for reasons that show awareness of the creature's qualities or the student's relationship with it.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express personal emotional connections to living beings through structured written sentences, giving reasons for their feelings.

competency.competency_text: Identifies needs of plants, birds, and animals, and how they can be supported (water, soil, food, care)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can name specific living things they feel connected to and articulate reasons for those connections that go beyond appearance.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Both sentences must be completed with a specific living thing and a reason. A response that names a creature but gives no reason has only partially engaged with the task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: reasons are specific and personal (e.g. 'because it sits on our gate every morning and makes a sound like a question'), showing genuine relationship with the creature. Weak: reasons are generic ('it is nice', 'it is beautiful') with no personal or ecological content.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who cannot write full sentences may complete the frames orally with the teacher noting the response. Children may use any language register they are comfortable with for the reason.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The sentence frames mirror the textbook's own reflection task and are designed to make personal connection expressible even for early writers.

assessment_items.question_text: Sana is listing animals from smallest to largest. She writes: ant, sparrow, cat, goat, cow. Which creature should she probably place BEFORE the ant in her list?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. The unit's skill is ordering living things by size using observation and prior knowledge. A mite or louse is smaller than an ant; a snail, crow, and dragonfly are all larger than an ant. Accept 'louse' or 'mite' as correct; the key is recognising that something smaller than an ant exists.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can order a set of living things by size, drawing on direct observation and prior knowledge to justify their ranking.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student places a crow (much larger than an ant) before it on a smallest-to-largest scale, suggesting size comparison between bird and insect has not been applied.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student places a snail before the ant, suggesting they have not compared snail and ant size carefully — a snail's shell and body together make it significantly larger than an ant.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student places a dragonfly before the ant, suggesting the comparison between flying insects of very different sizes was not made — a dragonfly is considerably larger than an ant.

assessment_items.task:
Draw and name one creature from each group below:
(a) Two legs
(b) Four legs
(c) Six legs
(d) Eight legs
assessment_items.scaffold: (a) Two legs — draw and name: ___ | (b) Four legs — draw and name: ___ | (c) Six legs — draw and name: ___ | (d) Eight legs — draw and name: ___
format_of_output: Four drawings, one per leg-count group
A name written next to or below each drawing
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit: all four groups have a correctly classified creature with a drawing and name. Partial credit: three groups correctly completed. Common error to watch: placing a spider (eight legs) in the six-legs group, or placing a dragonfly (six legs) in the four-legs group. Regional names for creatures are fully acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify living things by number of legs and represent that classification through named drawings.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply a leg-count classification system to living things they know, producing a named visual representation for each category.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Each section must have a drawing AND a name — a drawing without a name, or a name without a drawing, is incomplete. The name does not need to be spelled perfectly; phonetic approximations that identify the creature are acceptable.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: all four sections completed with correctly classified creatures and recognisable drawings, including at least one insect (six legs) and at least one arachnid (eight legs). Weak: only two or three sections completed, or insects and spiders confused.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find drawing difficult may write descriptive labels in place of drawings for one or two sections. Accept local or regional names for creatures.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The drawing-with-name format mirrors the textbook task exactly and allows classification to be demonstrated visually, making the assessment directly continuous with the activity.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wants to explain to their younger sibling what 'living in harmony' means. Using what you have learned in this chapter, write what you would say. Include: one example of how plants and animals depend on each other, one example of how humans and animals or plants depend on each other, and one thing a person can do to live in harmony with nature.
look_for: Gives a correct example of plant-animal dependence — for example, animals dispersing seeds, animals helping soil through waste, or a tree providing shelter and food to animals.

Gives a correct example of human-animal or human-plant dependence — for example, cows providing milk and humans providing shelter and food, or plants providing medicine and humans watering or protecting them.
Names a specific, actionable thing a person can do — providing water, keeping a bowl of grains, not harming creatures, visiting and caring for a plant, welcoming seasonal visitors.
The overall response reflects the chapter's core idea that dependence is mutual and care is a reciprocal responsibility.
assessment_items.annotation: This is the synthesis item. Award full credit when all three required elements are present and the mutual-dependence framing is clear. Award partial credit when two of the three are addressed. Regional examples are fully acceptable and expected.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent the web of mutual dependence between humans, animals, and plants through a visual map and articulate personal responsibility within that web.

competency.competency_text: Identifies needs of plants, birds, and animals, and how they can be supported (water, soil, food, care)

look_for: Gives a correct example of plant-animal dependence — for example, animals dispersing seeds, animals helping soil through waste, or a tree providing shelter and food to animals.

Gives a correct example of human-animal or human-plant dependence — for example, cows providing milk and humans providing shelter and food, or plants providing medicine and humans watering or protecting them.
Names a specific, actionable thing a person can do — providing water, keeping a bowl of grains, not harming creatures, visiting and caring for a plant, welcoming seasonal visitors.
The overall response reflects the chapter's core idea that dependence is mutual and care is a reciprocal responsibility.
